newsitem.title: USA: Oil prices hit six-year highs on supply worries.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices hit six-year highs on supply worries.

text.p: Oil prices soared to the highest levels since the 1991 Gulf War on Friday as cold weather swept into the northern United States and both traders and government officials worried about low heating oil stocks.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, November crude oil futures closed at $25.79, up 37 cents a barrel and the highest close since January 1991 in the middle of the Gulf War.
Friday's highest traded price was $25.85, beating the $25.70 post-Gulf War high set last April and matched this week.
The latest rally was a continuation of a bullish trend since the end of July that has been led by heating oil and has pushed crude oil prices up by almost 30 percent.
"It's a bullish close," said Rita Beale, an analyst at Fimat USA Futures.
Thomas Blakeslee, a trader and analyst at Cargill Investors Service, attributed Friday's gains to "continued Iraqi tensions, colder weather, lack of government action."
Analysts said the capture of a northern Iraqi town by one of the Kurdish factions from another faction Friday suggested an end to the fighting there was not imminent.
That in turn should mean a suspended Iraq-United Nations oil-for-food deal designed to allow up to $2 billion of Iraqi oil exports over six months is unlikely to be revived soon.

Meanwhile, weather forecasters predicted that a cold front that hit the Midwest earlier in the week would move into the Northeast over the weekend, dropping temperatures as much as 10 degrees below normal and increasing heating demand.

Heating oil futures lagged crude and gasoline gains Friday, probably due to nervousness ahead of a meeting between Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary and oil industry executives to discuss low stocks and the surge in prices.
But November heating oil still jumped 1.77 cents to close at 74.06 cents a gallon. November unleaded gasoline rose 1.41 cents a gallon to 67.94 cents.

O'Leary said on her way into the meeting that she would ask oil company executives whether they had extra refinery capacity to make heating oil. But with U.S. refineries running at between 93 percent and 95 percent of capacity in recent weeks, there doesn't appear to be much room for increased production.
The Department of Energy said this week that U.S. heating oil stocks were down 27 percent compared to the same time last year with key East Coast inventories off a huge 43 percent.

Traders also said concerns over political instability in Russia following the ouster of security chief Alexander Lebed by President Boris Yeltsin also helped underpin oil prices. Russia is the world's No. 3 oil producer.

Copper prices shrugged off the end to a one-day strike at a big Utah mine and smelter of Kennecott Corp. and finished higher on indications of strong Asian demand. December copper closed 0.65 cent higher at 91.55 cents per pound.
London Metal Exchange stocks fell a larger-than-expected 19,125 metric tons Friday to 172,425 metric tons, or below one month's global demand.

The London exchange's copper stocks have fallen sharply in recent weeks, but several analysts have said that much of the drawdown is going into off-exchange warehouses in China, rather than for industrial consumption.

"There are rising expectations the metal is being consumed in China," said Bette Raptopoulos of Prudential Securities. "But because of uncertainties, the market continues to move gingerly to the upside."
